Local authorities should use the allowance flexibly to meet individual needs, including where young parents may require additional essential items for themselves and their child.

The local offer should clearly explain:

who is eligible for the allowance

how young people can access it

how it is administered, including whether support is provided through direct purchases, instalments or lump-sum payments

the types of items it can be used to fund

any local processes for requesting support

any additional discretionary financial assistance that is available beyond the statutory allowance

The local offer should distinguish between support provided through the statutory leaving care allowance and any additional discretionary assistance offered by the local authority.

Where goods or services are purchased on behalf of a young person using the leaving care allowance, the local offer should explain how decisions are made and how the allowance will be allocated. This will help ensure transparency and enable young people to make informed choices about how their entitlement is used.

Education and training entitlements, allowances and bursaries

The local offer should explain financial support available to young people participating in FE, HE and apprenticeships, including:

the £3,000 apprenticeship care leavers’ bursary

the 16 to 19 bursary fund

the £2,000 higher education bursary

information on extended eligibility for foundation apprenticeships and level 7 apprenticeships, from age 21 to 24, for care-experienced young people, prisoners and ex-prisoners and people with an education, health and care plan

any local grants, travel assistance, equipment funding or other discretionary support, including for interview or work clothing

Further information is included in education, training and employment.

Benefits and entitlements

The local offer should provide information about benefits and financial entitlements that may be available to care-experienced young people and explain what support is available to help them access those entitlements.

This should include information about:

Universal Credit

council tax support and exemptions

disability-related benefits and support

housing-related financial assistance

support available through education, employment or training

local welfare support schemes and discretionary financial assistance

The local offer should explain:

what support is available

who may be eligible

how applications can be made

what help is available to complete applications and navigate the benefits system

Some former care-experienced unaccompanied asylum-seeking children (UASC) may be unable to access benefits as a result of having a “No Recourse To Public Funds” condition on their immigration status.

The local authority should assess the needs of the young person and gain a full understanding of their individual circumstances. A human rights assessment under schedule 3 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002 may need to be completed to determine which services should be provided. Schedule 3 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002 sets out the entitlements which migrants with No Recourse to Public Funds can access.

Former UASC and migrant children leaving care includes further information.

Junior individual saving accounts (ISAs)

Children who have been looked after continuously for 12 months or more and who are not eligible for a Child Trust Fund are entitled to receive a government contribution of £200 into a junior ISA.

The local offer should explain:

what a junior ISA is

who may be entitled to one

how young people can find out whether an account exists in their name

how they can access the account when eligible to do so

where they can obtain support if account information has been lost or if they were not previously aware of the account

Local authorities should ensure that care-experienced young people are aware of junior ISAs and understand how these savings can support them as they move into adulthood.

Case study: example of local practice

Derbyshire’s local offer provides practical, structured financial support to help care leavers manage money and transition to independence. This includes:

a £3,000 setting up home allowance for essential household items

support to purchase contents insurance and TV licences

full council tax exemption until age 25 for those living in Derbyshire (with the Leaving Care Service covering this for those living elsewhere)

Care leavers are also supported with:

budgeting sessions

tenancy‑readiness tools such as the Resettlement Passport

help to access their junior ISA

tailored support to ensure they are better off in work, including bridging payments while awaiting Universal Credit and discounts such as reduced water bills or temporary free Wi‑Fi

Legal duties

This section outlines the legal duties each local authority should consider as part of the local offer.

It includes details on:

corporate parenting, which includes a regional approach to the local offer

personal adviser support post-21

Staying Close support

domestic abuse

Corporate parenting

Every local authority is a corporate parent. The local offer is the clear, public statement of how these corporate parenting duties translate into practical, day-to-day support for care-experienced young people across areas such as housing, health, education, employment and participation.

Local authorities may wish to consider a regional approach to their local offer to ensure consistency in their corporate parenting duties and the support they offer to their care-experienced young people.

Corporate parenting principles includes further information.

Most schools and colleges provide information about the 16 to 19 bursary fund on their websites so links to these may be useful in the local offer. Students can also contact student support services for advice and guidance.

Apprenticeships

The local offer should include a dedicated section on apprenticeships, explaining that they combine paid employment with free training and are available from foundation level to level 7. Apprenticeships provide a route into skilled employment and can improve long-term career and earnings prospects.

Information should highlight that age eligibility for some apprenticeships has been extended for care leavers, including foundation and level 7 apprenticeships, from age 16 to 21 to 16 to 24.

The £3,000 apprenticeship care leavers’ bursary should be clearly promoted. The guidance should explain that the bursary is:

tax-free

not treated as income for Universal Credit purposes

paid through the apprenticeship training provider rather than the employer

Leaving care teams can provide confirmation of care leaver status when required. Care leavers should also be reassured that they do not have to disclose their care experience to their employer if they choose not to.

Where local authorities or local employers offer additional apprenticeship opportunities for care leavers, such as guaranteed interviews, tailored support or ringfenced vacancies, these should be included in the local offer with links to current opportunities.

The local offer could helpfully link to authoritative guidance on apprenticeships for care leavers, such as that available from the Moving On Up network.

Higher education

This section of the local offer should clearly state:

what support is available for students preparing for HE (pre-application)

how the local authority intends to support the young person while they are studying (participating)

how the local authority will support the young person once they have completed their course (post-graduation)

Local authorities should make clear what support is available at each stage of the process, including:

course selection: information on the wide range of options and flexible study modes available across level 4 to level 7 study, both within and outside the student’s home local authority, recognising that individual students’ needs and preferences will differ, and support to explore the use of contextual admissions, which are widely available across the HE sector

financial support: information on the statutory £2,000 HE bursary for care leavers, as well as the discretionary bursaries provided by many HE providers, and support to research and access any additional financial support that may be available

housing support: information on students’ entitlements to housing support while studying in HE and after graduation, including housing allowances, 365-day accommodation schemes and rent guarantor schemes, including where these are available to students studying outside their home local authority, as well as support to explore any additional housing support offered by HE providers

pastoral support: information on any entitlements to pastoral support while studying, together with signposting to relevant resources

support for postgraduate study and students graduating after their 25th birthday: clear information on whether the local offer includes support for students undertaking postgraduate study, and whether support is available where a course, whether undergraduate or postgraduate, will continue beyond the student’s 25th birthday, with local authorities encouraged to provide such support wherever possible

Employment

The local offer should include clear information about the general employment support available to care-experienced young people, including access to careers advice, links with local Jobcentre Plus services and wider employability assistance.

The local offer should:

set out any additional employment support that they or local partners provide for care-experienced young people, such as apprenticeships or pre-employment training and support offered by the authorities or businesses in the area, particularly where these opportunities are ring‑fenced for care‑experienced young people

ensure that care-experienced young people know about the apprenticeships care leavers’ bursary and how to claim it

set out where relevant third‑sector organisations might offer care-experienced young people specialist employment and skills support – this may include:

national and local charities providing mentoring

training or coaching

enterprise programmes

work‑readiness courses

sector‑specific opportunities for young people with care experience

outline the voluntary‑sector partners who provide a broader range of support, opportunities and expertise within the community, complementing the local authority’s own provision

set out opportunities to gain skills and experience through volunteering, community participation or short work placements

outline how care-experienced young people can benefit from the national Care Leaver Covenant, through which more than 700 public, private and voluntary‑sector organisations provide tailored opportunities for care-experienced young people, broadening the range of employment and skills pathways available and complementing the support offered locally

Case study: John Lewis Partnership – Building Happier Futures

The John Lewis Partnership is an employee-owned retail business, operating the John Lewis and Waitrose brands across more than 400 shops and online sites. Its Building Happier Futures programme supports care-experienced people into employment through a dedicated employability pathway and free online skills resources. Designed with input from people who have lived experience of care, the programme is available across all John Lewis Partnership locations.

Particular attention should be given to the support that care-experienced young people will need to take responsibility for their own health and to access appropriate services, including information and advice. A healthy lifestyle also requires proper attention to social, recreational and sports activities.

The local offer should:

set out local area services that educate on, support and enable good health and wellbeing

set out links to, or information about, universal health services that might be particularly relevant to care-experienced young people, and specific health, mental health and wellbeing services tailored to care-experienced young people

outline what support they provide directly to support care-experienced young people’s wellbeing, such as wellbeing walks, allotment groups or access to sport

Custody

When care-experienced young people spend time in custody, including in prisons, young offender institutions or secure training centres, local authorities retain important duties towards them throughout this period. Entering custody should not result in a break in the relationship between a care-experienced young person and their local authority.

Local authorities must maintain contact with eligible care leavers where they have duties to do so and should have arrangements in place to:

identify when a care-experienced young person enters or transfers between custodial establishments

establish where they are being held

maintain regular and meaningful contact throughout their sentence

The local offer should explain:

how care-experienced young people in custody will maintain contact with their PA and have access to pathway needs assessments and a pathway plan, which must include planning for support both during custody and on release – these plans must ensure that suitable accommodation and support are identified and prepared in advance of release

how regular contact will be maintained with care-experienced young people in custody, including by visiting them in person, such as:

what support will be available to maintain contact with family members, trusted adults or professionals

support to identify, develop and strengthen enduring relationships while in custody, including family finding services, mentoring and opportunities to build supportive networks that can continue following release

how leaving care services work with prisons, probation and other relevant agencies to coordinate support throughout custody and on release.

what financial support is available, including consideration of an appropriate and regular financial allowance and consideration of freezing entitlements to financial support (such as a setting up home grant) for the duration of their period in custody, so that these allowances can be available on their release – this should include how the local authority will provide financial advice, assistance and practical support to manage financial difficulties, address debt or financial exploitation concerns and prepare for financial independence on release

the wider support available to young adults during custody, including access to advice and advocacy, and plan for release and resettlement

information about local authorities’ arrangements for helping young people find and keep accommodation – see Support for young people leaving custody

Young parents

Young care-experienced parents often face isolation, insecure housing, poor mental health and barriers to education, training and work.

The local offer should set out how the local authority will help them build safe, stable family lives and positive relationships, recognising that many care-experienced young people lack strong support networks and may feel lonely.

Local authorities should recognise that some care-experienced parents may be reluctant to access maternity, health, early help or parenting support because of concerns about being judged or that asking for help may lead to involvement from children’s social care. Information should avoid language or practice that reinforces fear or stigma and should consider the use of trusted professionals, peer support and supported introductions to encourage engagement.

It should explain how care‑experienced young people who are parents can access support. This should include how they can:

access programmes that strengthen supportive relationships, such as family finding and mentoring – this should also be signposted and explain how young parents will be supported to access peer parenting groups, community networks and opportunities to build friendships and mutual support, including for those who are not currently caring for their children

receive help to continue or return to education, training or employment, including careers advice, childcare support and information on bursaries for FE and HE, and apprenticeships – education, training and employment has further details

access maternity, post-natal, health and mental health services, as well as support from family hubs, early help and parenting programmes offering practical guidance on infant care and child development

Former unaccompanied asylum-seeking children and migrant children leaving care

UASC are among the most vulnerable young people in the UK, often having experienced trauma, disrupted education, loss of family networks and long periods of instability. As they become care-experienced young people, many will continue to need emotional, practical and legal support, particularly if they lack family in the UK or are still navigating the asylum or immigration system. Unresolved immigration status can also affect their access to benefits, employment and education.
